utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for the day, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution together with Ms. Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone participating in the proceedings. On behalf of Mr. Perisic we have Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec and Daniela Tasic and Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith and Novak Lukic appearing in the courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, Mr. Hvaal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. 1 Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon sir, again. I'm now going to move to another subject, specifically what you testified at length during your stay in Sarajevo. In April 1992 you spent a few days in Sarajevo as far as I know; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps remember which period that was, whether it was towards the end of the month, do you specifically remember any event that took place while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, I was there in the beginning of the month rather than towards the end of it. I know this simply because it was before major hostilities broke out, but there were incidents of street fighting and general unrest, but major hostilities had not yet broken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of military formations existed in Sarajevo at the time, and how did they call themselves?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were still units of the Yugoslav Army. There were a number of paramilitary groups, some identifiable, but like paramilitary groups in many places, it's very unreliable to start making assumptions on who they are and where they are from, especially as an outsider. There was also at that point a very loosely organised form of what later became the Territorial Defence and then later on became the Bosnian government army. But at that stage it was in its very early infancy and it certainly didn't have a large noticeable presence. We heard about it more than we actually saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would really appreciate if you could give me shorter answers. I'm going to put to you very specific questions. When was the first time that you heard about the notion of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As referred to as the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that would have been sometime in the summer of 1992, but I cannot give you an exact date other than that. No, I can't give you anything more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have any direct contacts with any of the political leadership, the Bosnian government, or to be precise Muslim leadership, and by that I'm referring to Izetbegovic, Sedrenik, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we still talking about April here?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the entire period of your sojourn there.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met many of the political and military leaders in the area throughout my stay, yes. On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: These are the Muslim ones? Muslim leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what their personal religion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer whether or not they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When I speak about the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities, I'm referring to the authorities that had the status of political leaders of the recognised state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is why I made reference to the Muslims in my question. Did you visit the Main Staff of the Army of BH during any time while you were there? Did you enter the building itself and do you know where it is located?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the outset of the conflict in the summer of 1992, it was to my knowledge located in a bank building. That was the headquarters at least of the territorial army and it remained there for sometime, I can't tell you for how long. But, yes, I was there on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard the name of Jovan Divjak?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How about Stepan Siber?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic, Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see them personally?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least some of them. This is a long time ago, I can't tell you which -- I know I met Divjak, for instance, and Halilovic, but I can't be specific as to which ones I met and which ones I just heard about, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the 1st Corps of the BH Army was established? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you any direct, you know, answer to that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I say that throughout the war, or more precisely throughout the year 1993, there were about 70.000 members of BH Army in Sarajevo out of which 35 were deployed in the city itself, and 35.000 were outside of the city, would you agree with these figures?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no means of verifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this purely on the basis of your observations as a war correspondent reporting from various areas about your impressions that you get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The witness has answered question. He says he cannot verify those numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excepting I have a little question in my mind. When you say you cannot verify, you are leaving the impression that you have heard of the numbers only, you couldn't verify them. And I thought the intention was to say I don't know of those numbers and I thought, I'm not quite sure what the Defence counsel is doing, but I was expecting that to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that these numbers were ever mentioned relating to the strength of the BH Army stationed in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very difficult to answer because who would I have heard it from, and so in a war zone there are rumours flying, there's propaganda flying, there's numbers flying around the whole time, so if I had heard it or not, yes, most probably I have heard that number and a number of other numbers, but like I said I would have no means of verifying, so...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I agree. Having giving me the answer to the previous answer [sic], how would you able to distinguish between rumours and what you deem to be a fact or a reliable report that you should send forward?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In journalism you only state something as fact if it has been independently verified. That is, you know, common practice. If you don't know through independently verifying it or independent confirmation, you will have to quote someone as giving you the number. So you then say, you know, this is a number according to such and such a source.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo you often had an opportunity to see people dressed in civilian clothes but bearing arms and using weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not necessarily right, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in Sarajevo, did you ever see a person in civilian clothes armed with weapons?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone in civilian clothes shooting from a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there was a clear line of separation in Sarajevo between the two warring parties?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for anyone to cross from one side to another without any problems or difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were the residents of Bascarsija allowed to go to Grbavica without any problems whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allowed or able?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Freely without any problems, could they cross over?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody would try to stop them, but they would probably not survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were the residents of Grbavica able to come over to Bascarsija without facing any problems?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You gave your first statement to the OTP which is Exhibit P376 in March 1995 while the conflict was actually still in progress; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot discern from this statement where you gave this statement, I'm talking about the location, was that in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you give this statement?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Oslo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During 1995, if you can cast your mind back to that period, for how long were you away or absent from Sarajevo during that year?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you an exact number, but it would be maybe three or four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You would agree with me that with respect to certain events that your memory of these events was the most fresh in 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reasonably. I don't have a very good memory for detail, and I don't keep a diary, so I'm not a very good source when it comes to historical events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like now to ask you a question about some specific evidence -- incidents. You describe an incident which took place on the 23rd of June 1992 when a young boy was killed near Dobrinja. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had an opportunity to go through your statement before testimony, and if necessary we can put it on the screen. In paragraph 9 you said that there were no -- no military targets or clustered military targets at the location where this young boy was killed. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall my exact wording, but I would probably have said something like there was no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could the witness's statement be called up on the screen so he can see what Mr. Lukic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apology. Can we look at Exhibit 376, paragraph 9, that's in fact page 2 of the statement, I believe. The last paragraph, if we can zoom it in and just scroll it down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hvaal, do you see this? [In English] "There were no identifiable military targets in the area."

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that sounds more like what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reading from the B/C/S translation which probably caused some minor deviations. You were supposed to join a group of BH Army soldiers who were supposed to walk together with you to Dobrinja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were going there, anyway. I was supposed to walk with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many soldiers were in the group?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would estimate it to have been somewhere between a dozen and 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you did leave for Dobrinja with that group that night; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The wounded boy was first approached by BH Army soldiers who wanted to give him help; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I think to my recollection it was local civilians who ran into the -- ran to get to him first. I believe perhaps it was a relative of his. I think to my recollection it was an older man. I believe I have a photograph of this. I believe it was an older man who first ran out after he had been shot, yes. I don't think it was a military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you read the second sentence in paragraph 9, would that refresh your memory to the fact that the soldiers were also there trying to help? And this is your 1995 statement. I'm going to read it: [In English] "The soldiers who went out and gave him first aid were not fired upon."

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but these were not the first people to move out into the street. The boy was moved before he was given first aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But this was done by the soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the initial movement of the boy was done by a local civilian, to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that Mojmilo Brdo had been captured by BH Army in late June or early July of that same year when this particular event took place? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this incident took place immediately or during this offensive. Does that tally with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. When I crossed over Mojmilo hill that night and back out the following day, there was no offensive going on yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You continue by describing an attack on your vehicle which took place on your way back from Dobrinja to Sarajevo on the afternoon of the following day, that's paragraph 2, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, my question is, you were supposed to leave Dobrinja in a three-vehicle convoy as had been arranged from a doctor from Dobrinja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the first two vehicles left at 1600 hours and your vehicle left one half an hour later because your interpreter was late; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Times are not entirely accurate, but something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 16, you will find it that it reads: [In English] "We left twenty to thirty minutes after the other two ambulance..." [Interpretation] This was the basis for my question.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, what were you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, if you look from paragraph 16, maybe also paragraph 13, it reads as follows: [In English] "The first two ambulances left at about 1600 hours that afternoon." [Interpretation] Then paragraph 16 says that: [In English] "We left Dobrinja at about 1635 hours."

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says about 1600 hours, it says about 1635 hours and it says 20 to 30 minutes after the two ambulances, so like I said, I can't be precise about the times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no desire to lay any trap for you on this minutia, sir. Let me make it clear. Did you hear whether these first two vehicles had come under attack?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you were not part of that column as a third vehicle? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we obviously didn't move in convoy given that two vehicles had left sometime in advance, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at paragraph 20 on the next page, you describe another incident which took place in autumn of 1994 at Sedrenik and at paragraph 21 you say the following: [In English] "I was working on the job at the Kosevo Hospital on this day when I saw a young man in civilian clothing brought in." [Interpretation] Do you remember your account of that incident as well?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know whether this person had previously been involved in any combat action?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not there when he was injured. I could not tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that if not on a daily basis, you frequently went to the Kosevo Hospital in order to find out whether any incidents were happening or not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the people who were permanently in the hospital at Kosevo knew that you were a foreign journalist; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Judging by the photography published in the media and the consequences of the evacuation of children, did you gain some kind of popularity in Sarajevo? Did your name become a household name in Sarajevo, in a way?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the period while you were visiting the Kosevo hospital, were you able to see wounded soldiers of BH Army being brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that someone who was brought there -- or rather, do you remember ever being told that someone who was brought to the hospital wounded wearing civilian clothes had actually been a soldier, a fighter wounded in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that on the 20th of June 1992, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina declared a state of war and the general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's something contradictory here I want to ask you about. In paragraph 23, you say that: [In English] "... clearly marked with 'TV' in black letters on it to a position..." [Interpretation] referring to a vehicle. I'm asking you this because you mentioned orange markings. Did you have different vehicles that you used or is there a mistake here or in the next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had probably half a dozen different vehicles, and access to tape was limited so we had to use whatever colours we could come by. When we ran out of orange tape, we started using black tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On transcript page -- just a moment, 2268 -- or rather, we'll move on. In paragraph 24, you say that you had the impression you were deliberately aimed at because you were a journalist, that's the gist of what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember having this impression when a bullet whizzed past?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 24?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was deliberately aimed at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You remained there for a further 20 minutes together with the other people there; is that right? Try to remember without reading, please.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained there for about -- sorry, but if this is brought up on the screen am I allowed to look at it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would prefer to have your recollection, but if you can't remember then we'll jog your memory. I'm not asking you to be precise. I'm only asking you to try and recall approximately how long you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there for approximately 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I assume that there was a group of civilians there with you, or were you there on your own?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a group of civilians there with me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after this bullet was fired, no other bullets were fired in your direction subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it pertinent to change my location, but there were several more rounds that came in, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I ask you this because I read your statement and the last sentence of paragraph 24 is: [In English] "No further shots were fired at us after the shot that missed me." [Interpretation] Was your memory fresher when you were giving your statement then, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection now and regardless of what I read here, I believe that there were more shots fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had an opportunity of reading this statement before you made another statement and you introduced certain corrections, but you did not alter this sentence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think to be honest, it just -- you know, I didn't notice. It didn't register. Whether or not I remember it correctly, this is, as you know, a long time ago, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were also able to see this statement before you testified in the Galic case and again it remained unchanged?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would assume that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when asked by Mr. Saxon whether you abide by that statement in full, and whether you have had an opportunity to read it, you said yes, and that you did abide by it; is that correct? You said that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not want to correct anything in any of the paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, was that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a statement. You had nothing to change when you read this statement during your proofing a few days ago, you didn't alter any of the paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'll put a few questions to you concerning your second statement. That's P377. And you made it on the 14th and 15th of February 2001. And in this statement you described how you visited the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska for the first time in early 1993. Do you remember that that was when you first went to visit the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, my red lights apparently are not working, I will try to speak up. Perhaps if Mr. Lukic could bring the second statement on to the screen so the witness could see it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Could we please have paragraph 6. It's probably on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see? It's paragraph 6 in English. First try to remember, Mr. Hvaal, whether you visited the positions of the VRS around the city of Sarajevo in early 1993 for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of an -- sort of official organised visit, yes, but obviously in order to get in and out of the city, you would have to visit, you know, Bosnian Serb [indiscernible]. I had been in contact with Bosnian Serb military on many occasions before this when entering and leaving the city, but I think that would have been the first proper tour organised, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before that did you ask to join such an organised visit?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said here, to be precise, that you visited those positions about a dozen times during the war. When you testified on page 2252 you said eight to ten times. I'm not asking you to be that very precise but is that approximately this number of official visits to the VRS throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a more exact number than -- certainly not today and I can't give you an exact number than somewhere between 8 and 12 or about a dozen or in that region, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does this include your visits to press conferences, for example, at Pale, or are you referring exclusively to visiting combat positions?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- that would include visits to press conferences, but there were very few of those. Press conferences are not very interesting to photographers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when you last visited those positions in relation to the end of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been during the pullout from Grbavica after the Dayton agreement. I can't give you an exact date for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately in the course of 1994 and 1995 how many times did you visit the combat positions?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not beyond several times because the number I've given you includes the entire 1992 through 1995, so I can't give you -- it would have been several times, but I can't give you any more than that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When these visits were organised, as you told us, did you go on your own or were you accompanied by someone from your editorial office or were there other journalists from other media present?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would vary greatly, but it would normally be, and I stress, it would normally be a question of more than one organisation going in teams at the same time. But I did go alone as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 18 and 19 of this statement, you say that an offer was made for you to fire shots more than once during your visits. My question to you is you never agreed to do that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any other journalist or reporter agree to do that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no way of knowing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you able to see anyone from your group taking up a weapon in their hands while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall anyone taking a weapon in their hands, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you assume they would have actually given you a weapon but nobody actually asked for a weapon or took one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that. I have no way of knowing what goes on inside the head of somebody who says or asks me, offers me to use a weapon. Whether or not there's a genuine offer is something I can't have an opinion on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember as you described Kosevo hospital quite a lot, from what Serb positions is there a view from the Kosevo hospital? Can you tell us what those positions would be?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm no longer able to recall without looking at a map the names of the various hills around Sarajevo, I am afraid, so I can't give you a specific list of which hills, you know, gave a view of what part of the city. That would be pure guesswork.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll have to put a map on the screen, but first I'll ask you, when you were visiting the positions of the VRS, did you visit any positions from which you remember clearly seeing the Kosevo Hospital and the entrance to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Grbavica was a place in Sarajevo held by VRS forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Large parts of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Serb civilians lived there; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge there were some, but not many. I have -- I never saw large numbers of civilians in Grbavica, but I knew that there were some there, and when the withdrawal happened, there were civilians involved in that. Whether they had been there the whole time when the withdrawal happened or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the hospital on VRS-controlled territory either in Sarajevo or on Pale?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited what I believe was either a nursing home or an old-people's home. I believe a nursing home in the Nedzarici, perhaps. Yes, that would have been late in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you take any photographs there, did you report from there?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you ever at a sniper position of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, depending on your definition of a sniper position. I was in locations from which it was reasonable to assume that sniping was being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see sniper weapons there on the spot and the people manning the snipers?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by a sniper weapon?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a rifle or an automatic rifle with an optical sight apparatus.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen those on many occasion, yes, but that doesn't necessarily have any bearing on -- in our definition of sniping, the presence of an optical sight does not have anything to do with whether or not something is defined as sniping.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You received information about the sites from which snipers were shooting from UNPROFOR; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the United Nations military observers who were there as part of UNPROFOR, yes, but they were an independent, unarmed observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After visiting these locations at Grbavica, did you tell them what you had seen and where you had been?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Tell who?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Referring to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't -- as a general rule journalists don't report to any of the sides or elements involved in a conflict. The information that we have to give forward is basically the same as what we would do in our news stories and coverage and so on. Whether we shared information informally with UN personnel or anyone else, that would be a basis from one case to the other. And certainly there was no system for this, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we take the break now, please, and then I'll move on to another topic after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, we'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hvaal, while you were in Sarajevo did you visit the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on Mount Hum?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went on several trips up Mount Hum, but I don't think I remember -- I don't recall visiting proper positions. I think we were moving up trying to get there, trying to have a look at the situation, but to what extent there were positions, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just tell me briefly, I won't ask you about details, did you go up Mount Igman while it was held by the ABiH Army, while they were holding positions there, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you go up Mount Zuc where the ABiH had its positions, while they were there?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm having a -- I can't remember where that is at the moment, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were visiting the sniper positions at Grbavica, in paragraph 15 of the second statement which is now on the screen, you said that when you entered those premises where you found those people whom you said were snipers, that you saw holes in the wall, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These holes in the walls, were they a result of target practice or was it damage from fighting, from combat?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were neither of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of the two.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neither of the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us what caused those holes? What sort of holes were they?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were manmade, probably with sledgehammers or some sort of hard mechanical implement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know what purpose they were made for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Common way of building a sniper position is to use several --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Openings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several holes that are not in the -- in order to protect the sniper, sorry. This is -- it can't be explained in one sentence, I am afraid, this. A sniper is very rarely in the wall, on the outside wall of the building. He is usually at least one wall back. Now, there will be several openings in the outside wall and in the wall into the room where the sniper is so that there is a very, very narrow tunnel, imaginary tunnel through which he can shoot. This is to protect him so he can't be seen and the muzzle flash can't be seen and he can literally only see a very small area through those holes. That is a common way of building a sniper position if done by somebody who knows how to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But these were not openings intended for shooting through them?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the answer to that question is clear because Mr. Lukic asked the question in a negative structure, the witness responded yes, and I'm not quite sure what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does the answer mean yes, they are not intended for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are intended for -- to use for firing and looking. Observation and fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's try to listen to the question and answer it accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- well, we have the witness's clarification. The reason I ask is that in paragraph 15 it says "holes in the wall" and in 17 it says "loop-holes," and that's why I wanted to see whether these were one AND the same, but the witness is now saying that the holes were made for this purpose to be used as loop-holes?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, loop-holes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see loop-holes in paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reading from the Serbian where it says "holes in the wall." It says "holes in the wall" in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were accompanied by an officer who brought you there and who said that these were observation positions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall his exact words, but yes, it would have been something to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says this in paragraph 14, but I wanted to speed things up a little. While you were there, no one actually fired from those positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whenever you visited the positions of the Serb forces, no one was actually firing while you were at those positions? I'm not referring only to sniper positions, but all positions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the positions that -- do you mean the position that -- the actual position where I was or do you mean in the general vicinity of it, just that particular position? There would be small arms fire going out, but that's very difficult to say how close it's going out from, so on and so forth, but anything beyond -- are you talking about all kinds of weapons here? No. There would have been outgoing fire from fairly close by, yes, but normally small arms. I don't think I saw artillery pieces being fired right in front of me, no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Galic case on page 2258, line 24, you said that it was only towards the end of 1993 that it was possible to go to Grbavica, before that, there was heavy fighting there. Do you remember that that is how it was?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I mean, that would have been my assessment of it, it was too dangerous. Whether or not something would have gone badly wrong if you had tried it, I can't tell you that, that would be hypothetical. But I think the general assessment amongst the media at the time was that travelling to Grbavica was, you know, at the best of times dangerous, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to find the reference you are giving us. I'm not finding at page 2258, line 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2258, that's where it begins and then it continues on page 2259, from 1 to 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From 1 to 5. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in early 1994 so-called anti-sniping measures were introduced in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly -- I can't confirm the exact date on that, but at some point -- are you referring to the anti-sniping measures that UNPROFOR implemented?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Caca and Celo are? Are you familiar with these names?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, they were two, I don't know exactly how to describe them. A sort of mixture between paramilitary and criminal gang maybe, but again I don't know if they've ever been convicted of anything, but this is just an assumption. But they were known armed, they were known to have armed people and they were operating to some extent as part of the Bosnian government military. It was very -- these were not people that we had a lot to do with for very -- for good reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Ramiz Delalic, "Celo" was member of the 9th Mountain Brigade and Musan Topalovic, "Caca" was member of the 10th Mountain Brigade of the 1st corps of the BH Army? Are you aware of that, that they were members of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall having had that information or if I have, I have forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fine. Have you ever heard about the Silos camp in Hadzici?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: S-i-l-o-s, Silos.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you heard about a camp set up in the Viktor Bubanj army barracks?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard about the Viktor Bubanj army barracks, but a camp, no, again not to my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 35 to 47 of the same statement you described things that you saw in and around the Kosevo Hospital. Then you went on to describe having heard shots from mortars and small calibre weapons coming from the surrounding area of the hospital. That is in paragraph 41. Having said that, does that mean that you thought that these shots were fired by the BH Army? Because this particular area was under their control; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 42, you said that you sometimes had an opportunity to see a vehicle coming hastily, equipment was being unloaded, a few shells are fired and then the equipment would be loaded on the vehicle again and it would speedily move away; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there were both men in uniform and in civilians -- civilian clothes around those vehicles that you saw; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would assume so, yes. I don't recall -- certainly uniform, but it might very well be that there had been civilian clothes as well, especially in the winter because of the lack of warm uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the distance between the flat where you lived and the hospital, can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, I'm more interested to hear how far this vehicle that would come with the weapons, how far it was from the hospital roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they -- my flat in a straight line is probably say less than a kilometre, but this is, I -- you know, I mean the -- walking -- you could easily walk to the hospital in a relatively short period of time so it wasn't far away. But the road was not straight by any means, but less than a kilometre in a straight line, I would estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that the same street where the Belvedere Hotel is situated?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Belvedere Hotel is about 100 metres away from the hospital; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again it depends. The hospital is a very large area, many buildings there. Now, when I speak about the hospital, I would normally speak about the emergency unit, the trauma unit, which is further away, I believe, than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever take photographs of those scenes? I'm referring to the vehicles coming, dismounting the mortars, the shooting, et cetera, because you were able to see that from your window, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, this would only ever happen at night, and there -- it would be a pointless exercise to try and photograph it. Technically it would be very difficult, and to try -- soldiers who operate at night tend to not like having flashes from cameras fired at them. It's usually not a good idea to try to do that, as it were. So no, I don't think I ever photographed that sort of mobile artillery position, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 43 you say that you had heard rumours circulating around at the time that there was mortar fire coming from the hospital itself. Do you recall saying that and can you tell us who did you hear these rumours from, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- no, I can't give you a name of someone who said that. That would have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please don't try and guess. A minute ago you asked me when I asked you about the period in 1995 that you spent in Sarajevo, I'm going to ask you now about some specific events and I would like you to tell me if you were in Sarajevo during that time. Yesterday I asked you whether you were there in February 1994 when the event at Markale happened and you said you didn't. Now, do you recall, were you in Sarajevo in January 1994, which means a month before the Alipasino Polje incident where a number of children were killed?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: January 1994, I think I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember shooting photographs of that incident?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of which incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The shelling of Alipasino Polje, where a number of children were killed? Specifically on Klara Zetkin Street, if that's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I photographed that, no. But then I was not the only photographer there for the AP, so you know, it doesn't mean that we didn't cover it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the flea market in Bascarsija is?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there is one, but I couldn't describe to you where it is now, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember being in Sarajevo when an incident happened there in December 1994?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: An incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Involving shelling.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, but there were shells falling on Sarajevo every single day, so to remember one specific incident where a shell landed in a part of town where shells landed every day would be extremely difficult for somebody who was there for a long period of time. So I'm sorry. I would just be guessing to say if I could remember an incident from a month in a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to ask you any further questions about that. The photographs that we saw yesterday in this courtroom, can you remember, were these photographs published in the Serbian media, and if you do remember, can you tell us in which media?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I know that the story itself was reported, but no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 64, if we can please have it on our screens, you say that: [In English] "I must trust that I have no loyalty to any one faction within the former Yugoslavia." [Interpretation] Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you stand by it; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same statement, paragraph 3 at the beginning, which is on page 2, if we can also have it on the screen, you said - we'll have it on our screens shortly - [In English]: "If I were to try to explain the situation in Sarajevo to the third, uninformed party, I would say that I am an experienced observer of various war zones. This I feel equips me with an objective view of what I experienced in one of these places and I'm able to fairly compare one with another." [Interpretation] I suppose that you stand by this statement as well.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when I asked you, and I think that we agreed that one of the main features of the code of conduct of journalists is to be an objective -- to be objective and to report the truth; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that it's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have document 1D00-2697 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall giving an interview in January 2006 to some journalists with relation to the website of the Olympus company, and that rather long interview with you was published on this website?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to read just one sentence out to you, and I would then kindly ask you to give us your comment. That's on page -- actually, last page of the document. The journalist asked you: [In English] "Not only do I have the right to be political and subjective, I consider it's the duty to express myself freely through my images. There is no such thing as objective photojournalism." [Interpretation] Do you remember stating this?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is written by an advertising agency, so it might not be an entire -- entirely precise quote, but something to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Subjectivity begins already at the point of selecting what to photograph. Then comes the issue of timing, technical choice, editing and so on. The finished imagine will also be the photographer's personal messenger to the viewer." [Interpretation] Do you remember putting it like this?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again something to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Sarajevo, you also made a selection of what you were going to photograph and what images you are going to observe?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And through this conduit you conveyed your subjective message; right?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you Mr. Hvaal, I finished with my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Saxon. Just before you start, Mr. Lukic, what do you want to do with 1D00-2697?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move for it to be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How many pages is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A total of three pages. But I move that we only tender and admit page 3. The rest of the interview speaks more about the art of photography, but if Mr. Saxon believes that we can have the entire document, I have no objection to that. However, I propose that we only admit page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 3 of that article is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Mr. Saxon, sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hvaal, going back to my colleague's last question: "During your stay in Sarajevo, you also made a selection of what you were going to photograph and what images you are going to observe." You said yes. How did you make that kind of selection?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- as was pointed out earlier, it is impossible to conduct all covering objective journalism. When the television cameras in this courtroom focuses on somebody, somebody else is not seen in the frame. Now that in itself is subjective. It means that something is missing from the picture. Now, we know if somebody is sitting outside the frame doing this about whatever is being said. We simple don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can the record just reflect that the witness twirled his finger to the side of his head, please.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So there is an inherent process of selection. You cannot trust an image or an article or television footage or a website as such. The only element in the process of journalism that you can trust or choose to trust is the messenger. The people -- the messengers, the people who go to these places and report these things, the editors who edit the stories and put them out and do everything in their power to make this as accurate and reliable as possible. We cannot be in any way objective in the sense that as soon as you point your camera one direction, something else is not going to be in the picture. You cannot have 360-degree, 24-hour coverage of everything that goes on everywhere all the time. That would be objective, but then it would be impossible technically in every other way impossible. So yes, we do make selections. It is up to you, the viewers of this, to decide who is to be trusted and who is not. The best way that you can describe what is, in my eye or my view, a good journalist or a good photographer is somebody who can be described as a trusted or a reliable messenger. Somebody who brings you the essence, what is important. Somebody who makes those decisions, very difficult decisions as to what needs to be shown and what is not quite so important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for example, when you were working as a photojournalist in Sarajevo, what kinds of things did you feel or decide were important to be shown, needed to be shown?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be part of a larger decision-making process, not just based on the sort of individual incident, but also depending on what had been covered before, does it fit into our coverage, is it at a new aspect of it, shall we -- let's say there is yet another shelling with yet more casualties one day, nothing is new in this situation given that this goes on every day, so perhaps we should on that given day try and focus on something else, trying to put together a nuanced, how shall I say, as accurate an image as possible of what the story is, what is going on. But this judgement, these decisions have to be made from, you know, minute to minute because the situation changes all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Hvaal, changing the subject now, yesterday at page 2240 of the transcript, starting at line 6, Mr. Lukic asked you: "While you were still in Belgrade, before you went to Sarajevo, did you have occasion to follow the reporting of the Yugoslav media, the Belgrade media, or did you hear the comments of those media about reporting from Yugoslavia? " And at line 11 you said: "To some extent, yes." After you started reporting from Sarajevo in 1992, did you ever have occasion to go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On those visits to Belgrade, did you ever receive comments from members of the Belgrade media, journalists about your reporting from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe what kinds of comments you received?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- as I said also yesterday, it's a collaborative effort covering a situation like that. So the coverage out of Sarajevo would be closely coordinated with the Belgrade bureau and the Zagreb bureau and so on, so when you meet those colleagues there, obviously they are going to comment on your performance, we are going to comment on their performance. We are very much aware of what everyone is doing and trying to do in a situation like that. It's a very small club of people in these international media organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: But apart from the people working for the Associated Press, did you receive comments from journalists about your reporting from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Local journalists, you mean, local journalists in Belgrade, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly what kind of comments you received?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be largely positive, because -- well, yeah, largely positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Moving to another topic, the effect of the photo of Irma Ha dzimuratovic, which is Exhibit P380. At page 2244 of the transcript starting at line 12 Mr. Lukic asked you: "I concluded on the basis of your testimony that through the media this photograph caused quite a reaction, or at any rate, yielded the effect of having children treated abroad, so in a way it is that photograph that galvanized the public, as it were." And in your answer at line 16 you said: "I would say that initially it galvanized the media, and then from there on pressure was brought on in a number of western countries." Mr. Hvaal, when you say that this photograph of this girl galvanized the media, could you explain that a bit more, please. Galvanized the media to do what?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I think I described yesterday the frustration of repeatedly producing and distributing photographs and stories about all civilian casualties, but you know, including these children who cannot in any way seem to be combatants and therefore, in our opinion and I think any sane person's opinion, should be, you know, given medical treatment rather than be locked up inside a besieged city without the necessary facilities. That degree of -- you know, there wasn't much response in the international community to those things. Yes, there was an air lift, but it didn't take passengers out. There were a little bit of relief coming in, but there was no real effort in terms of the hospitals, in terms of, you know, the things that really needed to be do to help these children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay, but, Mr. Hvaal, we need to move more quickly here.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So galvanized the media to do what?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: To -- it basically meant that we focused -- pretty much all the media in Sarajevo at the time focused at a lot of their attention on making stories about this girl Irma, given that she seemed to be striking a nerve with the readers of newspapers, with television viewers and so on. So everyone piled on more pressure, wrote more stories and so on and produced more television footage in order to keep that snowball running, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: To use your term, "this snowball," can you estimate how long this snowball or this media campaign lasted?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can estimate it to have lasted for maybe a couple of weeks, maybe a bit more, until the actual first proper evacuation started happening. A few weeks, that's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Beginning when?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beginning on, well, probably the next day after the initial wire photographs went out, the ones that I took and other wire services took in August, and then the next day everyone was doing the story basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And roughly this period of or process of evacuations, roughly how long did the evacuations -- for how long a period of time were these evacuations carried out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Saxon is going beyond my cross-examination, beyond the scope of the cross, because I asked exclusively on the media, questions about the media and about the impact of photographs on public opinion, but I did not discuss the evacuation itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. -- in response to Mr. Lukic's question yesterday, Mr. Hvaal talked about how the photograph galvanized the media. And of course the result of that was these evacuations of children. Second of all, more specifically today, Your Honours, at page 12 of the line note line 7, my colleague precisely referred to the evacuation of children in a question to Mr. Hvaal he said: "Judging by your photography that was published in the media and the consequence of the evacuation of children, did you gain some popularity in Sarajevo? Did your name become a household name?" So I think the simple question asking approximately how long the evacuations went on for falls within the scope of re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I see Mr. Lukic is shaking his head but not standing up so I want to assume that you have quoted him correctly, therefore, I don't need to go and check the record. Then in that event, I'll, what is the word, dismiss the objection. Sorry, I'm using the wrong word there. I've forgotten the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Hvaal, approximately for what period of time did these evacuations of children take place?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a period of at least several weeks, possibly more than a month. It would have been -- it took awhile before it got going. There was a lot of politics and stuff going on and then there were several rounds of evacuations. So I would say it lasted for a period of several weeks, more than a month maybe even. Something like that, around a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the local and international media report about these evacuations?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was probably the most widely covered story out of the entire siege, I would say. A lot of media who were not normally in Sarajevo flew in specifically to cover the evacuation of the stories -- of the children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Mr. Hvaal, according to your testimony today, in page 33, point 5 to 23 you have described what I will try to gather in synthesis from you. In a way, you were saying that a image is both a message and a messenger, which is to say that the image is not only the vehicle of a message but also expressed in somewhat, some way the messenger, because you said first that the process of objectivity could not be understood fully and completely since there is an incompleteness in every image because as soon as you focused, then the surroundings or the totality of the universe is not reflected. So carries in itself an inherent incompleteness. That's one of the reasons you gave. Second, that in the selection it's up to the photographer to reflect part of himself or the totality of himself, his art, his skills, vision, artistic flavour, whatever, so in a way the objectivity of the image is only relative to the extent that it carries a message which could never be complete, and also carries the imprint of a personal actor who also could in the cover every possibility. But then from these two incompleteness, you reach the problem of trust that an image could be reliable as reflecting a portion of that incomplete reality and a portion of that incomplete selection to the extent that there are trusted messengers. Have I put you what you wanted to say in other words, to illustrate myself, can I examine later on your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have, I think it's P376, the statement of the witness that was made on the 28th of March 1995 on the screen, please, at paragraph 8. Mr. Hvaal, if you look at paragraph 8, you say in that paragraph "in the street outside of," and I believe that word should be heavily, "of the heavily damaged building where I was waiting, I heard the sound of two bullet impacts with only one or two seconds between them." Now, I'm not quite sure how heavily damaged this building was, but were you inside of this building at this time? And I tell you why I ask you is because you say, "I heard people screaming, we ran outside and found a boy of about ten sitting on the street." Am I right to assume that had been inside an enclosure somewhere out of which you ran?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume that. It would be very unwise to be out -- as a general rule you are not outdoors unless you have to in an area, in a situation like that. So and I was new to this area at this time. So I would assume that I would have been indoors, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you ran outside after the one or two bullet impacts had sounded.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been triggered by the screams, because the bullet impacts would not have been enough to make me go outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. But the screams could only come after the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They couldn't come before.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So after you went outside, there were no more bullets?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the immediate vicinity, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, at least not targeting this boy or the immediate vicinity of this young man?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing that was discernible, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks. Now then if you look at paragraph 10 on the screen again.

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There isn't one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, if we could get paragraph 10 come on the screen, please. Can you see that? You say in that paragraph: "The bullets came from an easterly direction from a place called Hrasno Brdo." And my question to you is how did you determine the direction from which the bullets came?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would have been a combination of the impact, I mean the track -- this boy had his chest completely perforated, the two rounds had gone through him, so it was possible to see the direction of the blood splashes on the ground where he had been hit. The blood would have splashed in the direction of the rounds coming through him. It's also because we knew where he was when he had been hit from the blood on the ground. You can then based on that, depending on what the buildings and trees and so on, you know, around that, you can estimate what can be -- you know, what angle can you -- what can you actually see from that position. So it would have been a combination of, you know, these factors. There may have been bullet impacts, but I would assume that it was primarily from the direction of the blood and from where because we knew exactly where he had been when he had been hit, which is quite rare. Normally there is some movement afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying he was hit and he fell down there and there was no movement until you arrived?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sitting on the ground. He had been hit by two high velocity, you know, large calibre rounds, which to a young boy is such a shock to the system. His chest -- you know, he was hit literally in the chest or in the abdomen, I think, in this area somewhere. That would be such a shock to the system, he would probably not be able to move after such an impact. One would be enough. Two would be a terrifying impact on a small boy like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. When that day you went to Dobrinja, how did you travel?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the way in I walked with a unit from the Bosnian military, Bosnian government military. They were going there carrying, as far as I know, supplies of some sorts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Walking, they were also walking?

utterances.speaker: MORTEN HVAAL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions arising from the question from the Bench? Mr. Saxon? Mr. Lukic? Thank you very much, Mr. Hvaal, that brings us to the conclusion of your testimony, let me just say thank you for you coming to testify before the Tribunal. You are now excused, you may go back home, please travel well back home. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your permission, I would also leave the courtroom at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we give you leave to leave, Mr. Saxon, just a small point that the Bench would like to raise with the parties with respect to the testimony of this witness. The witness testified on a number of incidents that are mentioned in his statement and the one photograph that he showed us. Are these scheduled incidents or are they not scheduled incidents or -- and if they are not scheduled incidents, what is the status of this evidence, given the decision that was made that the Prosecution will limit itself to scheduled incidents? I'm throwing it open to both parties to give the Bench guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, to answer your first question, no, this witness did not refer to scheduled incidents. These were not unscheduled incidents within the meaning of the Chamber's decision of May 2007, nor of the Trial Chamber's more recent decision of 31 October because they were not identified as such in the witness's 65 ter summary. The Prosecution felt that this evidence was relevant and probative to the issue of the level and kinds of notice that would have been aware -- that of would have been available to the accused about the events in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are neither scheduled nor unscheduled incidents, do I understand you correctly to be saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Do you have anything to say, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add, Your Honour. In relation to what is on evidence, I was concerned that the unscheduled incident that this witness was due to testify about should not be admitted into evidence. However, the witness did not testify to that and I cross-examined him on points I felt relevant for the Defence. My whole line of cross-examination concerned mainly evaluating the general objectivity of the witness's observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that the Trial Chamber is grateful that the parties are at one as to the status of this evidence. Thank you so much. You are now released, Mr. Saxon, you may leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas will be leading the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Thomas, you want to be changing the positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I will do that, thank you, Your Honour, and the Prosecution calls Colonel Koster who is a 92 ter witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is a?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Colonel Koster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is a?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
